analysis.one_liner: Blocks Medicare from testing a new way of paying for chemotherapy and other doctor-administered drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have killed a proposed Medicare experiment in paying less for drugs given in doctors' offices, died in two House committees with 22 cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Department of Health and Human Services from taking any step to finalize, implement, or enforce a March 2016 proposed rule that would have tested new ways for Medicare to pay for prescription drugs that patients receive in a doctor's office, such as intravenous chemotherapy. Medicare currently pays providers the drug's average sales price plus a 6 percent add-on; the proposed rule would have tested alternative payments aimed in part at paying less. Instead of a vote, the bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Specialty and brand-name drug manufacturers, and the oncologists, other physicians, and clinics that buy and bill Medicare for drugs administered in their offices, keep the existing payment formula — the drug's average sales price plus a 6 percent add-on — untouched, with no federal experiment that could have shifted how (and how much) Medicare pays them [S2] [S3]. Providers argued the current formula keeps costly drugs like chemotherapy available in community practices.

how_it_helps.text: Preserves Medicare's current Part B payment method — the drug's average sales price plus a 6 percent add-on — for drugs administered in doctors' offices, such as chemotherapy, by prohibiting HHS from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed Part B Drug Payment Model.

Stops a demonstration project that would have phased in alternative payment amounts and new tools for paying for these drugs, which providers feared would cut reimbursement to small and community practices that administer expensive medications.
A blanket prohibition rather than a redesign: HHS could not modify the model to address provider concerns and then proceed — the only option was to stop it entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers bear the cost of the status quo the bill protects. Medicare is the payer for these specialty drugs, and the proposed rule was an attempt to test payment methods that could pay less; a statutory prohibition forecloses testing any such savings, while leaving the price-linked 6 percent add-on — which pays providers more in dollar terms for prescribing costlier drugs — in place [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would have ended, without a replacement, the only federal experiment then proposed to test whether alternative payments could slow Medicare's costs for doctor-administered drugs — foreclosing potential savings for beneficiaries and taxpayers.

Providers had raised real concerns that the proposed model could cut reimbursement for small and community oncology practices and affect access to chemotherapy; a flat prohibition removed the ability to fix those design flaws and still test savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered providers certainty and protected the existing revenue formula, and the concerns about the demo's effect on small community practices were genuine. But the cost side is real too: it was an absolute prohibition on testing any alternative, not a fix of the model's flaws, so Medicare would have lost its chance to learn whether different payment methods could hold down what is now one of the fastest-growing drug categories for taxpayers. On balance, the bill traded away a chance at savings to protect current payments.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees and died when the 114th Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Larry Bucshon introduced the bill on April 29, 2016, joined by four original cosponsors, to prohibit HHS from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the March 2016 proposed rule known as the Medicare Part B Drug Payment Model.
The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and in May 2016 was referred to the health subcommittees of each.
No further action was ever taken: no committee markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Specialty drug makers and the physicians and clinics that bill Medicare for office-administered drugs, since the existing payment formula faced no legislative challenge. Beneficiaries and taxpayers gained nothing, because the payment experiment the bill targeted never moved forward either.

for.name: Rep. Larry Bucshon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit HHS from taking any action on the proposed Medicare Part B Drug Payment Model rule.

for.name: 20 of 246 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Dold, Boustany, Tom Price, and Shimkus.

for.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and community oncology providers
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the Part B Drug Payment Model proposed rule, which the bill would have blocked.

against.name: Department of Health and Human Services (Obama administration)
against.what_they_did: Proposed the Part B Drug Payment Model rule that the bill was written to prohibit, and had no reason to support blocking it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — 20 of the 22 cosponsors were House Republicans, with 2 House Democrats and a Republican sponsor — and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill protects Medicare's formula of paying the drug's average sales price plus a 6 percent add-on for drugs administered in doctors' offices, blocking a demonstration aimed partly at paying less for these drugs. Their gain comes at the expense of Medicare's budget and beneficiaries' cost-sharing.

industries.industry: Oncology and other physician practices and clinics that administer Part B drugs
industries.note: These providers bill Medicare for the drug price plus the 6 percent add-on, so the current formula pays them more in dollar terms for costlier drugs, and the proposed model would have changed that. They argued the change threatened the economics of community chemotherapy practices, so their interest in the bill was partly about revenue and partly about patient access.
